question: What does React.memo do?

options.text: It prevents mounting
It stores state in localStorage
It converts a component into a class
It can skip re-rendering when props compare equal

explanation: React.memo memoizes a component based on props comparison. Its own state and consumed context can still cause renders.

question: What is useCallback used for?

options.text: Storing a function in the DOM
Preventing a function from reading props
Memoizing a function reference while its dependencies remain unchanged
Executing a callback immediately

explanation: useCallback returns a memoized function reference. It can help when referential stability matters to memoized children or dependencies.

question: What is code splitting?

options.text: Splitting a component into DOM nodes
Breaking application code into smaller chunks that can be loaded when needed
Combining every file into one large bundle
Removing components manually

explanation: Code splitting reduces the initial JavaScript payload by loading parts of an application on demand.

question: What does React.lazy help with?

options.text: Loading a component dynamically when it is rendered
Memoizing props
Creating a global store
Validating forms

explanation: React.lazy loads a component through a dynamic import and is commonly paired with Suspense for a loading fallback.

question: What is client-side routing?

options.text: Routing SQL queries
Selecting CSS by screen size
Moving components to another server
Changing the displayed view based on the URL without a full document navigation for every route

explanation: Client-side routers map URLs to UI views and manage browser history. The server must still serve the app entry point for supported routes.

question: Why should an API request generally not start directly in the component body?

options.text: Requests can only be made from CSS
The browser blocks function requests
Rendering can run repeatedly, so the request could be started multiple times
Components cannot access fetch

explanation: Keep render pure. Start synchronization in an effect, user-triggered requests in event handlers, or use a data-fetching framework.

question: Why use TypeScript types for API response data?

options.text: They prevent network failures
They document expected data shapes and provide compile-time checking
They validate JSON at runtime automatically
They encrypt responses

explanation: TypeScript helps catch incompatible property access at compile time, but types are erased at runtime and do not validate untrusted JSON.

question: What is route-level code splitting used for?

options.text: Loading code for a route when needed to reduce the initial bundle
Encrypting route parameters
Making all routes public
Removing browser history

explanation: Lazy-loading route components can reduce initial bundle size, especially in applications with many feature areas.

question: Why can React.memo fail to skip a child render when data looks unchanged?

options.text: The child has a display name
The child returns JSX
The child has a CSS class
The parent may pass a newly created object or function prop on each render

explanation: Shallow comparison sees new object and function references as changed. Stable references may help when profiling shows a real problem.
